failures.title: Skoda CRLB Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: AdBlue System and NOx Sensor Faults - 2012-2020 models
items.whatHappens: The EA288 CRLB relies on an AdBlue injection system to meet Euro 6 emissions standards. The AdBlue pump, injector, or NOx sensors can fail, triggering warning lights, limp mode, and eventually preventing the engine from restarting once the countdown timer expires.
items.repairVsReplace: AdBlue component replacement or software resets typically cost £400-£1,500. This rarely necessitates a full Skoda CRLB engine replacement unless the failure has caused severe secondary damage. Read our full DPF and EGR failure guide.

items.title: DPF Clogging in Urban Use - 2012-2020 models
items.whatHappens: Like most modern diesels, the CRLB is sensitive to short, low-speed urban journeys. The Diesel Particulate Filter (DPF) can become clogged with soot, leading to restricted exhaust flow, loss of power, and frequent forced regenerations.
items.repairVsReplace: DPF cleaning or replacement costs £400-£1,200. If chronic clogging has led to excessive backpressure and turbocharger or EGR damage, a reconditioned CRLB unit may be the most reliable long-term solution.

items.title: EGR Cooler Leaks and Carbon Buildup - 2012-2020 models
items.whatHappens: The Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) cooler can develop internal leaks, allowing coolant to mix with exhaust gases or enter the intake tract. This causes rough running, white smoke, and potential hydrolock if severe.
items.repairVsReplace: EGR cooler replacement is a standard repair (£500-£1,000). If coolant ingestion has warped the cylinder head or scored the cylinders, a full engine replacement is required.

failures.goodYearsLine: The EA288 CRLB is generally considered more robust and refined than its EA189 predecessor, with improved thermal management and fewer catastrophic timing chain issues, though strict adherence to service intervals remains critical.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the Skoda CRLB
variants.intro: The CRLB is the specific 150hp (110kW) calibration of the EA288 2.0 TDI family. It is frequently confused with older EA189 variants (such as the CRBC) or the slightly different CNHA variants found in later facelift models.

relatives.description: The earlier EA189 2.0 TDI that the CRLB replaced, carrying the legacy of Dieselgate software issues and more frequent EGR/DPF failures than the updated EA288 architecture.

The newer EA288 Ultra efficiency revision that succeeded the CRLB, featuring further refinements to the AdBlue and emissions systems for improved fuel economy, though sharing the same fundamental 2.0 TDI architecture.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Skoda CRLB - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Skoda CRLB engine is only advisable if the seller provides documented proof of regular motorway use and recent AdBlue/DPF servicing. Without this history, the risk of inheriting a clogged emissions system is too high. Learn more about sourcing used engines.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned Skoda CRLB is the most balanced choice for most owners. A quality rebuild will replace the vulnerable EGR cooler, refresh the AdBlue pump and injectors, and ensure the DPF is clear, effectively eliminating the engine's primary design weaknesses. Explore reconditioned engines.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified if the original CRLB suffered catastrophic failure due to EGR-induced hydrolock or severe turbocharger contamination. An upgraded rebuild should include the latest revision of the emissions hardware and reinforced cooling components to prevent recurrence. View rebuilt engines.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Buying through our network ensures your replacement Skoda CRLB is installed by vetted UK specialists, backed by a minimum 12-month warranty, with nationwide delivery options for both supply-only and full supply & fit packages.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The CRLB is commonly found in Skoda Octavia Mk3 and Superb Mk3 models, which typically hold a market value of £4,000-£12,000 depending on age and condition. Because the replacement cost is generally well within the vehicle's retained value, a reconditioned engine is a financially sound investment, and replacement is considered highly viable across almost all examples. However, for older sub-£4,000 examples (like early Octavia Mk2 or Superb Mk2), we strongly advise evaluating scrap or part-exchange value before committing.

items.answer: The CRLB was fitted to the Skoda Octavia Mk3 (5E), Superb Mk3 (3V), Kodiaq, and Yeti as the 2.0 TDI 150hp badge from 2012 to 2020. It is the 150hp (110kW) calibration of the VW Group's EA288 2.0 TDI family, and you should always verify your exact engine code via the V5C or engine bay sticker before ordering parts. items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Skoda CRLB engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Skoda CRLB is strongly recommended over a used unit unless the seller provides documented proof of regular motorway use and recent AdBlue/DPF servicing. A proper recon replaces the vulnerable EGR cooler, refreshes the AdBlue pump and injectors, and ensures the DPF is clear, whereas used units risk inheriting a clogged emissions system that will fail shortly after installation. items.question: How do I know if my car has the CRLB and not the CRBC or CNHA?
items.answer: You can confirm your engine code by checking the sticker on the engine block, reviewing your V5C registration document, or using our free registration lookup tool. The CRLB is the 150hp EA288 calibration, distinct from the older EA189 CRBC or the efficiency-tuned CNHA Ultra, and fitting the wrong revision will result in ECU mismatch, incorrect turbo plumbing, and immediate limp mode due to differing emissions architectures. Check your registration now to confirm your engine code
